extraction_notes.note: The numerical schemes are stated as one implicit time step given by coupled variational equations; they were emitted as algorithms without algorithm_step children, since any step would coincide with an equation node. Only the decoupled form AP2 was split into its two subdomain solves.

Numbered equations named in the text (Poincare-Friedrichs inequality (3.9), polarization identity (4.4)) were retyped as external theorems per the equation-retyping rule; the surrounding sentence ('There exists a constant $C_p$ such that') is not part of TP1's span.
Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2 are environments whose proofs only cite CHL12 and Galdi, so they are marked origin external; their citation proofs are kept as paper proof nodes.
Tables of convergence rates, figures, and descriptive discussion of vortex patterns in Section 6 were not extracted; only the explicit numerical conclusions became claims with rigor numerical.

nodes.name: Atmosphere-ocean (fluid-fluid) coupling problem with nonlinear interface condition
nodes.statement:
Consider the $d$-dimensional ($d=2,3$) polygonal or polyhedral domain $\Omega$ in space that consists of two subdomains $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$, coupled across an interface $I$, for times
$t\in [0,T]$. Coupling problem is: given  $ \nu_{i}>0 $, $f_{i}:[0,T]\rightarrow H^{1}(\Omega_{i})^d,u_{i}(0)\in
H^{1}(\Omega_{i})^d $ and $\kappa \in \mathbb{R} $, find (for $i=1,2$) $u_{i}:\Omega_{i}\times [0,T]\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ and $p_{i}: \Omega_{i}\times [0,T]\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (for $0<t\leq T$)

 










\begin{eqnarray}
\partial_{t}u_i -\nu_i\Delta u_i+u_i \cdot \nabla u_i + \nabla p_i &=&  f_i \qquad \mathrm{in}\ \Omega_i, \\
-\nu_i \hat{n}_i  \cdot \nabla u_i \cdot \tau &=& \kappa |u_i - u_j|( u_i - u_j )\cdot \tau \quad \mathrm{on}  \ I \ \mathrm{for} \ i,j = 1,2, \ i \neq j \,  , \\
u_i \cdot \hat{n}_i  &=&0 \qquad \mathrm{on} \ I \ \mathrm{for} \ i,j = 1,2, \\
\nabla \cdot u_i &=&0 \qquad  \mathrm{ in } \ \Omega_i, \\
u_i(x,0)&=&u_i^0(x) \qquad\mathrm{ in }\ \Omega_i , \\
u_i&=&0 \qquad\mathrm{ on } \ \Gamma_i = \partial\Omega_i\setminus I , \end{eqnarray}
where $|\cdot|$ represents the Euclidean norm and the vectors $\hat{n}_i$ are the unit normals on $\partial \Omega_i$, and $\tau$ is any vector such that $\tau\cdot\hat{n}_i=0$. Here $u_i$, and $p_i$ denote the unknown velocity fields and pressure. The parameters are $\nu_i$ kinematic viscosities, $f_i$ the body forcing on the velocity, $\kappa$ the friction parameter (frictional drag force is assumed to be proportional to the square of the jump of the velocities across the interface).
nodes.statement_short: Two Navier-Stokes subdomains coupled across interface $I$ by a quadratic friction (drag) interface condition with parameter $\kappa$.

nodes.name: Interpretation of the projection tensor as large scales
nodes.statement:
In \eqref{alg4}, the tensor $\mathbb{G}_i^{\mathbb{H},n}$ represents the large scales of $
abla u_{h,i}$, defined by $L^2$-projection of $
abla u_{h,i}^n$ on $\Omega_i$ into the large scale space $L_i^H$ (see Definition ef {defpro}). Hence, the difference $\mathbb{G}_i^{\mathbb{H},n}-
abla u_{h,i}^n$ represents the resolved small scales. This way, the GA-VMS method \eqref{BE7}-\eqref{alg4} introduces the additional viscous term into the momentum equation acting only on the resolved small scales. We note that the $L^2$- projection terms for $\mathbb{G}_i^{\mathbb{H},n}$ can be discretized implicitly or explicitly in time. We will consider here the computationally attractive explicit discretization, and refer the reader to \cite{jokaya3,JK08} for further discussions on explicit vs. implicit discretizations of $\mathbb{G}_i^{\mathbb{H},n}$.

nodes.statement_short: $\mathbb{G}_i^{\mathbb{H},n}$ is the $L^2$ projection of $\nabla u_{h,i}^n$ onto $L_i^H$, so the added viscosity acts only on resolved small scales; treated explicitly in time.

nodes.name: Choice of large-scale space and eddy viscosity
nodes.statement: In GA-VMS formulation of \eqref{BE7}-\eqref{alg4}, the large scale spaces $ L_i^H$ and $\nu_T$ parameters must be chosen. The first approach is to define $L_i^H$ using in lower order finite element spaces on the same mesh, provided that finite element spaces $(X_{i}^h,Q_{i}^h)$ are high enough order. Second approach is to define $L_i^H$ on a coarser grid than $(X_{i}^h,Q_{i}^h)$, see, e.g., \cite{jokaya3,JK08}. Herein, we will use the first way which is the most common choice in geophysical problems. Thus, we choose $ L_i^H$ to be piecewise polynomials of degree $k-1$. The choice of the parameter is $\nu_T=h$ is typical for various artificial viscosity-type models.

nodes.statement_short: Take $L_i^H$ as degree-$(k-1)$ piecewise polynomials on the same mesh and $\nu_T=h$.

nodes.name: Choice of the coarse mesh size $H$
nodes.statement: We note that while the larger choice of the coarse mesh size $H$ provides more efficient projections into large scale spaces $L_i^H$ and reduces storage, the accuracy of the solutions decreases. For $k=2$, the typical choice is $H=O(h^{1/2})$ for the projection-based VMS. This choice is obtained from balancing terms in the convergence analysis. In our numerical studies, we will use single mesh, that is $H=h$. Although, it is expensive (particularly in $3d$) because of storing the velocity gradient will be the same as storing three additional velocities, it is also good way of programming since there will be less bookkeeping. As we will show later this choice also provides good accuracy.

Altogether, the behavior of the discrete solutions observed here is in agreement
with the analytical results: GA-VMS is a first order accuracy model of atmosphere-ocean interaction.

nodes.statement: Clearly, GA-VMS performs better than GA in terms of conservation of the total energy.

nodes.name: GA-VMS captures energy transfer between domains (numerical)
nodes.statement: Figure \ref{fig:total_energies_separately} illustrates that this expectation has been met by GA-VMS since the total energy in the atmosphere increases beyond the initial energy input while the exact opposite happens in the ocean.

nodes.name: GA blows up while GA-VMS stays stable (numerical)
nodes.statement: Figure \ref{fig:stability} illustrates that the solution with GA starts blowing up around $t=25$ while GA-VMS produces stable results all the way up to final time $T=100$.
